source_user: Explain how continuous batching changes between training and inference. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Treat this as a phase-specific comparison: training normally processes a fixed batch with teacher forcing and forward/backward passes, gradients, and optimizer state, whereas inference serves independent requests and autoregressive decode can use continuous batching. The mechanism is dynamic iteration-boundary admission/retirement during decode; training examples generally remain part of the planned batch because removing one sequence changes gradient aggregation and padding/packing semantics. A boundary is that some inference systems also batch prefill, and training systems may use packing, so the label alone does not determine behavior. State model, sequence lengths, hardware, precision, parallelism, runtime, and batch/admission policy; measure forward/backward and optimizer memory/time separately from prefill, TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and KV memory. Do not infer training speed or convergence from serving tokens/s.
risks: Training and serving phases can be conflated, making throughput claims incomparable.

source_user: Explain how continuous batching changes between training and inference. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching is chiefly an inference scheduling pattern, not a drop-in replacement for a training batch. During training, teacher-forced examples contribute jointly to a loss and gradients, typically through a planned microbatch; in autoregressive inference, requests advance one token per decode iteration and finished requests can be replaced at iteration boundaries. That replacement is the concrete mechanism. The boundary is workload and implementation dependent: prefill may be batched differently, and changing membership during gradient computation can alter effective batch size or gradient semantics. source_user: Explain how continuous batching changes between training and inference. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: In training, continuous admission of examples is not equivalent to continuous batching in serving: examples are usually selected into microbatches for teacher forcing, backpropagation, and gradient accumulation, while inference requests can be admitted or retired between decode iterations. The mechanism to call out is that a completed inference sequence releases decode work and a waiting request may enter the next iteration; training has no analogous safe retirement once its forward/backward graph and loss contribution are defined. A boundary is phase: inference prefill may have different batching and training may use sequence packing, so results cannot be transferred across phases. Specify effective batch size, accumulation, lengths, hardware and precision, then measure per-step forward/backward/optimizer time and memory versus prefill/decode latency, throughput, KV memory, queueing, and correctness.

source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: The intuition ‘continuous batching makes training behave like serving and therefore always improves utilization’ is misleading. In inference decode, iteration-boundary retirement and admission can reduce idle slots caused by different request lengths. In training, a microbatch normally must preserve its examples through forward, backward, and gradient reduction; replacing one example early could invalidate the intended loss weighting or synchronization. The boundary condition is whether the workload is decode, prefill, or training and whether the implementation supports safe packing or dynamic shapes. To test a claim, hold model, hardware, precision, lengths, and resource limits fixed, then measure training step/phase time, memory, and convergence separately from TTFT, inter-token latency, queueing, throughput, KV memory, and failures. A utilization increase alone is not proof of better outcomes.

source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: ‘Continuous batching always lowers latency because the device never waits’ is false. The boundary condition is the phase and scheduler/resource regime, especially KV capacity and arrival load.
